Source consultation dialogue:
[doctor] Hi there! How are you doing today?[patient] Hi, I'm alright. I've got this issue with my left forearm, though.[doctor] What seems to be the problem?[patient] There's this lesion on my left forearm that's been growing pretty fast. It's been about two months now.[doctor] I see. Can you tell me more about it?[patient] Yeah, it's been getting bigger continuously. Sometimes it bleeds and itches, which makes it really hard to work, especially in the sun. It also gets irritated when my clothes rub against it.[doctor] That sounds uncomfortable. Have you tried any treatments for it?[patient] I've tried some over-the-counter stuff, but nothing seems to work.[doctor] Hmm, okay. Could you tell me a bit about your medical history?[patient] Sure, I have chronic eczema, which I've had since 2015, and allergic rhinitis that started in 2017.[doctor] Thanks for that information. Anything else in your medical history?[patient] No, that's about it.[doctor] Alright. And how about your social habits? Do you smoke or drink?[patient] Yeah, I smoke about 10 cigarettes a day, and I drink frequently, around 3-4 beers a day.[doctor] Okay. How about physical activity and your diet?[patient] Physical activity is mostly related to my job, and my diet isn't great. I eat a lot of carbs and processed foods.[doctor] Got it. Let’s review some other systems. Have you noticed any weight loss, fever, or fatigue?[patient] No, none of those.[doctor] Any swelling in your lymph nodes?[patient] No, I haven't noticed any swelling.[doctor] Alright, let’s take a look at your vitals.[doctor] Your blood pressure is 130/85 mmHg, heart rate is 76 bpm, respiratory rate is 16, and your oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. You are afebrile.[patient] Okay, sounds good.[doctor] Let's examine the lesion on your left forearm.[doctor] This lesion is irregular in shape and has variegated colors including black, brown, and red. It's approximately 8 mm in diameter and it does bleed with slight pressure. There are no signs of secondary infection.[patient] Is that bad?[doctor] It’s concerning. I’m going to check your lymph nodes now.[doctor] No enlarged lymph nodes detected in the axillary or cervical regions. That’s a good sign.[patient] Okay, what's next?[doctor] Based on your symptoms and the appearance of the lesion, I'm concerned it might be malignant melanoma. We need to take immediate steps.[patient] What does that mean?[doctor] We’ll start with a surgical intervention. We'll perform an excisional biopsy with 1 cm margins to ensure complete removal of the lesion and obtain samples for histopathological analysis.[patient] Alright, that sounds serious.[doctor] We’ll also refer you to Dr. Ana Martinez, an oncologist at the nearest regional hospital, for further evaluation and potential adjuvant therapy. Depending on the biopsy results, we might discuss immunotherapy options.[patient] Okay, what's immunotherapy?[doctor] It’s a type of cancer treatment that helps your immune system fight cancer. But we’ll discuss it in more detail once we have the biopsy results.[patient] Understood. What else do I need to do?[doctor] We’ll also order an MRI of your left forearm to evaluate the extent and depth of the lesion and check for potential local spread.[patient] Okay, an MRI. Got it.[doctor] We’ll schedule a post-surgical consultation to discuss the biopsy and MRI results and formulate a comprehensive treatment plan. We should also initiate routine skin surveillance every 4 months due to your occupational sun exposure to monitor for any new or recurring lesions.[patient] Okay, that makes sense.[doctor] We’ll also talk about lifestyle modifications. It’s essential to reduce tobacco and alcohol use. I’ll provide counseling on adopting a balanced diet and incorporating protective measures against sun exposure, like wearing long sleeves and using sunscreen.[patient] Yeah, I know I need to cut down on smoking and drinking.[doctor] We’ll also give you information on smoking cessation programs and nutritional counseling available within the community health services.[patient] Okay, I’ll look into that.[doctor] You’ll return to the clinic in one week for a follow-up and to discuss the biopsy results.[patient] Alright, I’ll be back in a week.[doctor] Lastly, I’ll provide education on the importance of skin self-examination and early medical consultation for any new or changing skin lesions.[patient] Got it. I’ll keep an eye on my skin.[doctor] Great. Any questions for me?[patient] No, I think that covers it.[doctor] Excellent. Take care, and we’ll see you next week.[patient] Thanks, doctor. See you then.

[doctor] Good morning, Julie, how are you today?[patient] Good morning, Doctor. I'm doing well, thank you.[doctor] That's great to hear. So, what brings you in today?[patient] I wanted to discuss starting birth control, mainly for contraception and also to help regulate my menstrual cycle.[doctor] Alright, I understand. Do you have any current health issues?[patient] No, I don't have any health issues right now.[doctor] Got it. How are your menstrual cycles currently?[patient] They are pretty regular, but I do get moderate cramps.[doctor] And how do you manage those cramps?[patient] I usually take ibuprofen, and it works fine for me.[doctor] Okay. Do you have any current sexual partners?[patient] No, not at the moment.[doctor] Understood. Would you like to discuss safe sex practices for the future?[patient] Yes, that would be helpful.[doctor] Great. Let's go through a review of systems first. Have you experienced any unintentional weight loss or fatigue recently?[patient] No, none.[doctor] Any headaches, vision changes, or hearing difficulties?[patient] No, none of those either.[doctor] How about chest pain, palpitations, or edema?[patient] No, I haven't had any of those symptoms.[doctor] Any shortness of breath or cough?[patient] No, my breathing is fine.[doctor] Have you had any abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or changes in bowel habits?[patient] No, my digestion is normal.[doctor] How about your genitourinary system? Any abnormal discharge?[patient] No, just the regular menstrual cycles and moderate cramps.[doctor] Any joint pain or stiffness?[patient] No, my joints are fine.[doctor] Any headaches, dizziness, or abnormal sensations?[patient] No, none of that.[doctor] Do you have any history of depression or anxiety?[patient] No, I don't.[doctor] Alright. Let's move on to your vitals. Your blood pressure is 120/75 mmHg, heart rate is 72 bpm, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, and temperature is 98.6°F. Your oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. All normal. Now, I'll do a quick physical exam.[patient] Okay.[doctor] You appear well-nourished and well-developed, and you're in no acute distress. Your head is normocephalic and atraumatic. Your oropharynx is clear and there’s no cervical lymphadenopathy. Your heart has a regular rate and rhythm, with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Your lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally, no wheezes, rales, or rhonchi. Your abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no hepatosplenomegaly. You have full range of motion in all extremities, no deformities or edema. Neurologically, you are alert and oriented, and your cranial nerves II-XII are intact. Finally, your skin shows no rashes or lesions.[patient] That all sounds good.[doctor] Yes, everything looks normal. So, for your primary concern of contraception and menstrual regulation, I will prescribe you birth control pills. These will contain ethinyl estradiol 30 mcg and levonorgestrel 150 mcg. You’ll take one tablet daily for 28 days.[patient] Thank you. That sounds good.[doctor] You're welcome. Along with the birth control pills, it's important to discuss safe sex practices, including the use of condoms to prevent sexually transmitted infections.[patient] Yes, that's very important to me.[doctor] I'm glad to hear that. Maintaining a healthy lifestyle is also crucial. Do you exercise regularly and follow a balanced diet?[patient] Yes, I do. I try to stay as healthy as possible.[doctor] That's excellent. Keep up the good work. We’ll schedule a follow-up visit in 3 months to evaluate how you’re tolerating the birth control pills and their effectiveness.[patient] Okay, that works for me.[doctor] If you experience any severe headaches, visual changes, chest pain, or leg pain/swelling, please call the clinic immediately.[patient] I will. Thank you for the heads-up.[doctor] You're welcome. I’ll also provide you with educational materials on healthy lifestyle choices and safe sex practices. Do you have any other questions or concerns?[patient] No, I think you covered everything.[doctor] Great. Remember, it’s important to adhere to the medication regimen. If you have any issues or concerns, don’t hesitate to reach out.[patient] I will. Thanks again, Doctor.[doctor] You're welcome. Take care, Julie, and I'll see you in three months.[patient] Sounds good. Have a great day.[doctor] You too. Goodbye.

[doctor] Hi John, how are you doing today?[patient] Hi, Doctor. I've been better. I've been dealing with some pretty severe muscle weakness and atrophy lately.[doctor] I see. Can you tell me more about when you first noticed these symptoms?[patient] It started about six months ago. I've noticed it's been getting worse over time.[doctor] Can you describe how these symptoms have been affecting your daily activities?[patient] Well, it's been really tough to walk, lift objects, and just move around in general. Even the simplest tasks have become difficult.[doctor] I understand. This must be very challenging for you. Have you noticed the weakness and atrophy in any specific areas of your body?[patient] Yes, mainly in my arms and legs. It's especially noticeable in my quadriceps and biceps.[doctor] Hmm, okay. Are there any other symptoms you've noticed that might be related?[patient] Just the weakness and difficulty in performing daily activities. It’s really impacting my quality of life.[doctor] Alright. Let's go through a quick review of your systems. Any issues with your neurological system, like muscle weakness?[patient] Yes, definitely muscle weakness.[doctor] How about your musculoskeletal system? Besides the muscle atrophy, any difficulty walking or lifting objects?[patient] Yes, both. Walking and lifting objects have become really difficult.[doctor] Okay. How about your endocrine system? Any known conditions there?[patient] I have Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, and I'm currently on Metformin for that.[doctor] And your cardiovascular system? Any issues there?[patient] Yes, I have hypertension. I’m taking Lisinopril for it.[doctor] What about your respiratory system? Any known conditions?[patient] I have Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD). I also smoke about a pack of cigarettes a day.[doctor] Okay, thank you for sharing all that. Let's move on to your vital signs. Your blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg, heart rate is 78 bpm, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, temperature is 98.6°F, and your SpO2 is 94% on room air. [patient] Okay.[doctor] Now, I'll perform a physical examination. You're alert and oriented, and in no acute distress. Let's check your muscle strength. [doctor] (performing muscle strength test) I see there's decreased strength in both your upper and lower extremities.[patient] Yes, I can feel that.[doctor] And there is visible muscle wasting in your quadriceps and biceps. Let's check your gait.[doctor] (observing gait) I notice you have an abnormal gait and difficulty maintaining balance.[patient] It’s become harder to walk steadily.[doctor] We’ll need to wait for the results of your biochemistry panel, blood glucose levels, and thyroid function tests. Also, we’ve scheduled an MRI of the affected areas for next week to determine the extent of muscle wasting.[patient] Okay, sounds good.[doctor] Based on your symptoms and our examination, we suspect muscle wasting and atrophy, not elsewhere classified. This could be due to various reasons, including neuropathic or myopathic conditions secondary to your Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus or other metabolic disorders.[patient] That makes sense. What do we do next?[doctor] First, we’ll start you on Vitamin D supplementation: 50,000 IU, oral, once weekly for 8 weeks. Continue your current medications: Metformin 500 mg (oral, twice daily) and Lisinopril 20 mg (oral, once daily).[patient] Alright.[doctor] We’ll also need to perform some investigations, such as a biochemistry panel, blood glucose levels, and thyroid function tests. The MRI will help us identify the extent of the muscle wasting.[patient] Got it.[doctor] Additionally, I’ll refer you to physical therapy for specialized muscle rehabilitation.[patient] Okay, that sounds good.[doctor] I’d also recommend some lifestyle modifications. Nutrition counseling to adopt a high-protein and balanced diet, a personalized exercise plan to improve muscle mass and strength, and smoking cessation support to help you quit smoking.[patient] I know I need to quit smoking. I'll try.[doctor] That’s a great first step. Also, better sleep hygiene can improve your overall health.[patient] I’ll try to work on that.[doctor] We’ll schedule a follow-up appointment in 8 weeks to reassess your symptoms and evaluate your response to treatment. We’ll also review the results of the tests we’ve ordered.[patient] Okay, I’ll be here.[doctor] If your symptoms worsen or if new symptoms arise, please return to the clinic immediately. Maintain a daily log of your activities, diet, and any changes in symptoms to discuss at the next visit.[patient] Will do. Anything else?[doctor] Just remember to contact the clinic with any questions or concerns about the treatment plan. [patient] Alright, thank you, Doctor.[doctor] You’re welcome, John. Take care, and see you in 8 weeks.[patient] Thanks, see you then.

Source consultation dialogue:
[doctor]: Hi there Ms. Doe, what brings you in today?[patient]: Hi, Doctor. I've been having some pretty bad pain in my left shoulder.[doctor]: I see. How long has this been going on?[patient]: It's been about nine months now. It started off mild but has gotten worse over time.[doctor]: I understand. Can you describe the pain for me? Is it constant or does it come and go?[patient]: It's pretty constant. It gets worse with activity, especially when I'm trying to do things around the house like dressing, cooking, or even simple chores.[doctor]: That sounds tough. Have you noticed any other symptoms like limited range of motion, clicking sounds, or stiffness?[patient]: Yes, all of those. I can't move my shoulder as well as I used to. It clicks sometimes and feels really stiff.[doctor]: Got it. Have you had difficulty sleeping because of the shoulder pain?[patient]: Yes, sleeping has been really hard. The pain wakes me up sometimes.[doctor]: Alright. I see from your records that you have hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Are those conditions well controlled with your medication?[patient]: Yes, I take Amlodipine for my blood pressure and Atorvastatin for my cholesterol. They seem to be working fine.[doctor]: That's good to hear. Any family history of medical conditions that we should know about?[patient]: My mother had arthritis, and my father had heart disease.[doctor]: Thanks for that information. Are you allergic to any medications?[patient]: Yes, I'm allergic to Penicillin.[doctor]: Okay, thank you. Now, let's talk about your social history. Are you currently working?[patient]: No, I'm retired. I used to be a school teacher.[doctor]: Do you smoke or drink?[patient]: I don't smoke. I have a glass or two of wine per week.[doctor]: How about your diet and exercise?[patient]: I try to eat a balanced diet that's low in sodium, and I do some light walking every day. But my shoulder pain has really limited my exercise routine.[doctor]: Understood. Now, let's check your vitals. Your blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg, heart rate is 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 per minute, and your temperature is 98.6°F. [patient]: That sounds normal, right?[doctor]: Yes, those are all within normal ranges. Let's move on to a physical examination of your shoulder. Does it hurt when I press here on your glenohumeral joint?[patient]: Yes, that’s tender.[doctor]: How about your range of motion? Can you lift your arm like this?[patient]: No, that's really difficult and painful.[doctor]: Okay, I’m going to perform a couple of tests. First, the Hawkins-Kennedy test. Does this cause pain?[patient]: Yes, it does.[doctor]: And now the Neer’s sign. How about this?[patient]: Yes, that hurts too.[doctor]: Alright, based on your symptoms and physical examination, it seems like you have primary osteoarthritis of your left shoulder. [patient]: Oh, I see. What does that mean?[doctor]: It means that the cartilage in your shoulder joint is wearing down, causing pain and stiffness. It's a chronic condition but manageable with the right treatment.[patient]: What do I need to do?[doctor]: First, I’ll prescribe you some medications for pain—Acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed, and a topical Diclofenac 1% gel to apply on your shoulder four times a day. [patient]: Okay, that sounds manageable.[doctor]: I’ll also refer you to a Physical Therapist, Dr. John Smith, for shoulder rehabilitation. You’ll have sessions twice a week for eight weeks.[patient]: Will that help?[doctor]: Yes, physical therapy can significantly improve your range of motion and reduce pain. Additionally, I'll recommend some gentle stretching exercises and continuing with your light walking. Heat and ice packs can also help manage symptoms.[patient]: That sounds like a lot, but I can do it.[doctor]: Great. We’ll also schedule a follow-up appointment in eight weeks to reassess your pain and function.[patient]: Do I need any tests?[doctor]: Yes, I’m ordering an X-ray of your left shoulder—three views: anterior-posterior, lateral, and axillary. This will help us assess joint degeneration and rule out other pathologies.[patient]: Okay, when will I get the X-ray?[doctor]: We’ll set that up for you today before you leave. It’s important to understand that osteoarthritis is a chronic condition, and adherence to your treatment and rehabilitation plans is crucial.[patient]: I understand. I’ll follow the plan.[doctor]: Excellent. If you have any questions or concerns before the follow-up, don’t hesitate to reach out.[patient]: Thank you so much, Doctor.[doctor]: You’re welcome, Ms. Doe. Take care and see you in eight weeks.[patient]: Will do. Thanks again!

Can you tell me more about when the acne started and how it has been affecting you?[patient]: Sure. It started about a year ago and has been getting worse. I get these painful cystic lesions on my chin and jawline, and they seem to get even worse during my menstrual cycle. It's really affecting my self-esteem and my daily activities.[doctor]: That sounds really frustrating. Have you tried any treatments in the past?[patient]: Yes, I've been prescribed various treatments, but honestly, I haven't been very consistent with them. And those I did use regularly didn't seem to help much.[doctor]: I understand. Consistency with treatment can be tough, especially when you're not seeing the results you want. Do you have any other symptoms or issues that you think might be related to your acne?[patient]: Well, besides the acne, I've been having a hard time sleeping. I feel restless and it's difficult to fall asleep. Also, the stress from the acne is really getting to me.[doctor]: I'm sorry to hear that. Any other health conditions we should be aware of?[patient]: Yes, I have hypothyroidism.[doctor]: Got it. Let's go through a few more details. Have you noticed any changes in your skin besides the acne, like hyperpigmentation or scarring?[patient]: Yes, definitely. There are dark spots and some scars from previous breakouts.[doctor]: Alright. Based on what you’ve told me, it sounds like your acne has a significant hormonal component. Have you noticed any other related symptoms, like irregular menstrual cycles or hair growth in unusual places?[patient]: No, my periods are pretty regular, and I haven't noticed any unusual hair growth.[doctor]: Okay, let’s review your systems to cover all bases. For skin, you have numerous inflamed nodules and cystic lesions, especially on your chin and jawline, with hyperpigmentation and scarring. For endocrine, you mentioned hypothyroidism. How about your sleep; you said it's poor and restless?[patient]: Yes, I have a lot of trouble falling asleep and staying asleep.[doctor]: And for your psychiatric state, you mentioned stress and low self-esteem due to the acne?[patient]: That's correct.[doctor]: Let's check your vital signs now. Blood pressure is 122/78 mmHg, heart rate is 72 bpm, respiratory rate is 16 bpm, and your temperature is normal at 98.6°F. Your Body Mass Index is 26 kg/m2.[doctor]: Now, I will do a physical examination. I see numerous inflamed nodules and cystic lesions on your chin and jawline. There is also some hyperpigmented macules and post-inflammatory scarring. Fortunately, I don't see any signs of secondary infection. Everything else seems normal.[doctor]: I’m going to order some tests. We’ll do a hormonal profile to understand the cyclical nature of your acne better. This will include checking your testosterone, luteinizing hormone (LH), and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels. We’ll also do a biochemistry panel to assess your baseline electrolytes and renal function before starting you on a new medication.[doctor]: Based on everything we’ve discussed and observed, it looks like you have moderate to severe acne, possibly with a hormonal component. We need to rule out conditions like Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS), but we'll treat it as hormonal acne for now.[doctor]: For your treatment, I’m prescribing a topical gel called Adapalene 0.1%. Apply it to the affected areas once nightly. I’m also starting you on an oral medication called Spironolactone, 50 mg, to take once daily. This should help with the hormonal aspect of your acne.[patient]: Okay, thank you. How soon will I notice any changes?[doctor]: It might take a few weeks to see noticeable improvements. We’ll have you come back in 6 weeks to evaluate how the treatment is working and check for any side effects.[doctor]: In the meantime, I recommend increasing your water intake and avoiding high glycemic index foods, which can exacerbate acne. Improving your sleep hygiene and increasing physical activity can also help manage stress and overall health.[patient]: Okay, I can do that.[doctor]: It’s really important to stick to the treatment regimen for it to be effective. I’ll explain the potential side effects and what to watch out for. The hormone profile test will help us understand the cyclical nature of your acne better. Also, if you’re having trouble affording the medications, there are financial aid programs available.[patient]: That’s helpful to know. I’ve had issues with my insurance before.[doctor]: In that case, I encourage you to seek support from a healthcare navigator who can assist with insurance and prescription access. Maintaining a daily skincare routine with gentle, non-comedogenic products is also crucial.[patient]: I’ll definitely look into that. Thank you.[doctor]: You’re welcome. Do you have any other questions or concerns?[patient]: No, I think you’ve covered everything.[doctor]: Great. Let’s get started on these treatments and see how you’re doing in 6 weeks. Take care![patient]: Thank you, Doctor.
